newsitem.title: USA: U.S. say halts sale of alleged pain relief device.
newsitem.headline: U.S. say halts sale of alleged pain relief device.

text.p: Federal officials have halted sales of "The Stimulator," a $79.95 device advertised as a pain reliever on TV by pitchmen including motorcycle daredevil Evel Knievel, a U.S. Attorney said Friday.
Officials contend the hand-held device is essentially a camp stove igniter that emits an electrical spark, Emily Sweeney, U.S. Attorney for Ohio's northern district, said in a statement.
A spokesman for a firm that distributes the Stimulator said it emits a charge to provide electromagnetic stimulation and that testimonials from customers say it alleviates pain.

"It's a registration issue, not a safety or effectiveness issue," Ed Davila, a lawyer for the firm, Akron, Ohio-based Universal Management Systems, Inc., said. He said the company would fight the injunction "in every way legally possible."

In 1995, the U.S. Attorney's office seized 17,000 of the devices, which it estimated had a $1.3 million market value, but Universal continued to market and sell the device, Sweeney said. Now, she said, unless the FDA approved it, further sales were prohibited.
The U.S. argues that selling the Stimulator violates a 1977 federal food, drug and cosmetic law, Sweeney said.
Sweeney said the injunction required Universal Management to destroy, under FDA supervision, any devices in its possession and if requested by the FDA, to recall them.
Another firm, Natural Choice, Inc., and two individuals, Paul M. Monea and Paul A. Monea, are named as defendants.
Davila said Paul M. Monea was a principal in Universal Management and Paul A. Monea was an employee but has left the company. Natural Choice was another distributor, he said.
